01

What this is

Working, live demo

The problem it solves and the one-sentence version.

Today an email plugin suggests which Salesforce record a message belongs to, and by the team's own estimate it lands on the correct one about forty percent of the time. The hard cases are exactly the ones that matter: a client with several open bookings, or a planner whose one email address is connected to dozens of them.

This system catches every incoming email and text message and files it on the correct booking automatically. It matches on more than the sender's address. It reads the message itself: the event date, the names, and the kind of event. When one booking clearly fits, the message attaches on its own. When the answer is not clear, the message waits in a review queue where a person confirms the right booking. A wrong guess never saves itself.

02

How it works, end to end

Five steps, no magic.

  • 1. A message arrives the way it already does. A client emails or texts. For email, each mailbox is set to copy each message to a receiving address in Salesforce. That copy step is one Gmail setting per person. For texts, the phone provider hands each message straight to Salesforce the moment it arrives.
  • 2. It identifies the sender and gathers every open booking connected to that address, including the planner case where one address touches many bookings across different contacts.
  • 3. It reads the message. The event date in any format people actually write, the names mentioned, and the kind of event. Each detail is compared against each candidate booking.
  • 4. It decides, carefully. One clear winner attaches automatically with its reasoning saved. No clear winner, and the message waits in the review queue with a ranked list and plain-English reasons for a person to confirm. Trivial replies like "ok" and "thanks" are filtered out entirely.
  • 5. Everything stays in Salesforce. Every captured message becomes a permanent record in the org, tied to its booking, visible to managers, and reportable like any other Salesforce data.
Also captured

The team's outgoing replies can be captured through the same copy setting, so the conversation on a booking shows both sides, not just the client's half.

03

The walkthrough

Every clip is the real system

Each step below plays as a short clip. These are real messages moving through the real system in a demo org with fictional data.

A real email, sent and matched

An ordinary Gmail message is written and sent to the receiving address. Seconds later it appears in the review queue, already attached to the right booking, with its reasoning shown in plain English.

The planner case: one address, several bookings

A planner writes about a holiday party. It ranks both of their open bookings, picks the one whose date and event type the message actually names, and shows why. Address-only tools cannot make this call.

A text message, arriving live

A text reaches the business number and the phone provider hands it straight to Salesforce. The sender's number is typed differently than the number on file and it still matches, because formatting is stripped before comparing.

Junk stays out

A two-word reply comes in. It recognizes it as noise and never logs it, so the queue holds real work only.

The safety net and the settings

Match strictness, the junk phrase list, watched mailboxes, and an optional safeguard for single-booking senders, all on one settings page, adjustable in-house with no code and no vendor.

The alternatives, fairly

Match My Email is a well-rated product and Einstein Activity Capture is free. Both match on the email address alone. The hard cases above are where that stops working.

Said plainly

These tools are the right choice for simple address-based syncing. The reason this build exists is that the matching problem here is not simple, and the message content is the only place the answer lives.

05

Data, storage, and ownership

Checked against real org data

The questions we checked before making claims.

  • Storage. Each captured message costs a fixed sliver of Salesforce data storage. At roughly three times the current monthly email volume, permanent retention adds about a quarter of a gigabyte per year against several free gigabytes available in the org today. Decades of headroom, and old records can be archived by policy if ever wanted.
  • Ownership. The code lives in the business's own Salesforce org, along with the data. Nothing depends on an outside service staying in business for that history to remain intact.
  • Visibility. When something needs adjusting, the full history of what happened is visible in the org, so the cause can be found and fixed directly rather than waiting on a vendor's support queue.
06

What comes later

Planned, not yet built

Honest scope: what Thursday's demo does not include.

  • Sending text replies. Receiving texts works from day one. Sending replies requires a carrier registration step for businesses that takes days to a few weeks, so it lands as a follow-on phase, filed on day one.
  • Mailbox-level polish for production. Attachment capture, automatic setup for each team member's mailbox, and notification preferences get finalized during the production build.
  • Optional intelligence add-on. A later phase can layer smarter language understanding on top of the same system. The current matching is deliberately simple, explainable, and fast.
